title: LMCache: Vendor-Neutral KV Cache Management Layer with Tiered Offload, Non-Prefix Reuse, and PD Disaggregation
event_hint: Official LMCache documentation landing page describing its role as an engine-independent KV cache management layer for LLM inference.
problem: KV cache is normally a temporary, engine-internal state: it is lost when the inference engine crashes (fate-sharing), cannot be reused across requests/sessions/engines, and forces expensive re-prefill — especially painful for long-context agentic, multi-turn, and RAG workloads where TTFT and throughput suffer.
mechanism: LMCache runs as a standalone daemon process separate from the inference engine, so KV cache survives engine crashes. It moves KV cache out of GPU memory into a tiered storage hierarchy (CPU RAM → local SSD → remote backends) and exposes a unified pluggable interface over many backends: CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS. CacheBlend extends reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any prompt position and selectively recomputing tokens for quality recovery. A SERDE interface allows pluggable compression/quantization (e.g., TurboQuant), token dropping, and custom serialization. For PD disaggregation it transfers KV cache from prefill to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP via transport layers such as NIXL.

evidence.claim: LMCache is a standalone daemon that manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process so KV cache is not lost on engine crash (no fate-sharing).
KV cache is offloaded into a tiered hierarchy (CPU memory, local storage, remote backends) enabling reuse across requests, sessions, and engine instances to cut repeated prefill and improve TTFT.
evidence.source_locator: Key features > Persistent, tiered KV cache offloading and reuse

evidence.claim: Supported storage/transport backends include CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS.
evidence.source_locator: Key features > Pluggable storage and transport backends

evidence.claim: CacheBlend enables non-prefix KV reuse by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt and selectively recomputing tokens for quality recovery.
PD disaggregation transfers KV cache from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP through transport layers such as NIXL.
evidence.source_locator: Key features > PD disaggregation and KV transfer

evaluation_context: Documentation landing page (no benchmark tables). Documented adoption signals: AMD MI300X agentic workload benchmark (2026/05), multi-node P2P CPU memory sharing moved to production (2026/01), LMCache × CoreWeave accelerating inference for Cohere (2025/11), NVIDIA Dynamo integration (2025/09), 5000+ GitHub stars (2025/08), joined PyTorch Foundation (2025/10). Listed research backing: CacheGen (KV cache compression/streaming), CacheBlend (cached knowledge fusion), 'Do LLMs Need a CDN?'.
limitations: Explicit (page-level): documentation is under reconstruction; some sections may be incomplete. Explicit: no quantitative numbers (TTFT speedup, hit rate, compression ratio, transfer bytes) on this landing page. Inferred: the multi-node P2P / NIXL / RDMA transports are cluster-local; the page does not address WAN cross-region placement, consistency overhead, or RTT/bandwidth tradeoffs that the briefing's cross-region question requires.
project_relevance: Highly relevant. LMCache is a central KVCache cross-node/cross-engine reuse layer: its multi-node P2P CPU memory sharing and NIXL/RDMA transports map directly onto KVCache cross-node transfer and CXL/disaggregated-memory themes; CacheBlend's non-prefix reuse and CacheGen compression map onto the 'compression / incremental transfer / prefetch' sub-question; and its Redis/Mooncake/S3 backends are natural candidates for DPU/SmartNIC-offloaded or cross-region shared stores. Multi-engine reuse also intersects with Agent cache / tool-result sharing, since cached context could in principle be shared across serving instances.
